title: Outliers
objective: After this level you can spot an outlier and decide whether it is a mistake to fix or a real case worth keeping.
summary: An outlier sits far from the rest and can pull the mean. Investigate it: a proven mistake is corrected or removed; a real case, like Robert Wadlow's 272 cm, is kept.

cards.headline: A height survey lists someone at 272 cm. Typo, or record?
cards.body: It could be a slip of the keyboard. Or it could be Robert Wadlow, measured at 272 cm in 1940. Values that stand far from the rest are called outliers, and the job is working out which kind you have found.

cards.headline: Far from the rest
cards.body: An outlier is a value notably different from the rest of the data, and it matters because it can bend your results. Swap one retirement age of 60 for 81 in Level 12's list of 11, and the mean jumps from about 56.6 to about 58.5. The median? Still 57. Before you trust any average, look for values sitting far out on their own.

cards.headline: A mistake? Fix it
cards.body: Some outliers are simply bad data: a number typed wrong, an experiment run incorrectly. If a survey of schoolchildren lists a child aged 123, somebody slipped. When a value is shown to be an error, you correct it if you can, or take it out.

cards.headline: Real? Keep it
cards.body: Other outliers are true. Wadlow really was 272 cm (8 ft 11.1 in), the tallest man in medical history with irrefutable evidence. Deleting him would make the data tidier and wrong. That is why outliers get investigated before anyone touches them, and are not deleted just for being inconvenient. A real outlier can be the most interesting value you have.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: investigate an outlier before you touch it. Mistakes get fixed; real cases stay.

cards.headline: Outliers: investigated
learned: Outliers sit far from the rest
They pull the mean, not the median

options.label: The most common value in a set
Any value above the mean
options.rationale: Plenty of ordinary values sit above the mean; an outlier is extreme.

options.label: A value notably different from the rest
The value in the middle of the list

questions.explanation: An outlier stands far from the rest of the data, like a retirement age of 81 in a list of 54 to 60.

questions.prompt: Match each outlier with what to do about it.
questions.explanation: A child aged 123 and a number typed wrong are mistakes, so you fix them. Robert Wadlow really was 272 cm, so you keep him.

questions.prompt: One retirement age in a list changes from 60 to 81. Which average barely notices?

options.label: The mean, because it is an average
options.rationale: The mean counts every value, so it jumps from about 56.6 to about 58.5.

options.label: Both move by the same amount
options.rationale: The mean moves; the median stays at 57.

options.label: Neither: one value cannot matter in a list of 11
options.rationale: One value moved the mean by about 2 years.

options.label: The median, which only needs the middle value

questions.explanation: As with a friend group where one person earns far more, the mean counts every value but the median only needs the middle.
